themes.theme: an attacker-supplied field in the options object turns the polish stage into unbounded work — the MAX_POLISH_WORK budget is advisory, not authoritative
findingSummaries: `resolveWantPolish` honours an explicit `polish: true` without ever consulting `MAX_POLISH_WORK`, so the single most expensive input on the default path — the exact 33 s case the constant was introduced to kill — is still reachable by setting one boolean.
themes.remediation: Make the budget the authority rather than a default-only heuristic: `resolveWantPolish` must return false (or, better, clamp the iteration count so the modelled work fits) whenever `polishWork(n, k, iters) > MAX_POLISH_WORK`, including when the caller passed `polish: true`. Honouring a direct instruction is not worth a 33 s stall the constant exists to prevent — if the request must be respected, respect it by deriving iterations from the budget, which is the follow-on already recorded in graph.ts's MAX_POLISH_WORK comment. Then delete the n-only `POLISH_MAX_N` mirror in app/src/state/useBuddyGraph.ts so there is exactly one gate and it cannot drift again.

themes.theme: an attacker-supplied field in the options object turns the polish stage into unbounded work — the MAX_POLISH_WORK budget is advisory, not authoritative
findingSummaries: `checkedIterations` validates the TYPE of `polishIters` (integer, non-negative, finite) but never its MAGNITUDE, so any large finite integer passes the guard verbatim and becomes the polish loop bound — the sibling one boundary over from the Infinity case the guard was written for.
themes.remediation: Stop validating the budget in isolation and bound the WORK instead: clamp the resolved iteration count so `polishWork(n, k, iters) <= MAX_POLISH_WORK`, i.e. `iters = min(checkedIterations(...), floor(MAX_POLISH_WORK / (n * m)))`. That single change subsumes the existing type checks (Infinity/NaN/negative all fail the same comparison) and closes both this and the `polish: true` sibling with one rule, so the polish stage has one ceiling rather than a type guard plus a bypassable flag. Replace the [Infinity, NaN, -1, 1.5, -Infinity] case table with the invariant below.

themes.theme: a size gate that runs after the work it is meant to bound — Constraints.fromTags builds O(n^2) pair keys inside the constructor, before validate can refuse anything
findingSummaries: `Constraints.fromTags` takes `n` entirely on faith — unlike `degreeOf` in the same file, the `Graph` constructor and `validate`, all of which guard it — and then runs an unguarded `for (i < n) { for (j < n) }` materializing one Set key per same-tag pair, so the cost is paid before any cap can be consulted.
themes.remediation: When the tag UI lands (not before): validate `n` against MAX_ROSTER/MAX_CONSTRAINED_N as the first statement, then pre-count group sizes in one O(n) pass and refuse against a pair cap (sum of C(size,2)) BEFORE the double loop runs, and reject non-finite/NaN tag values by normalizing them to null.

gating.failure: Measured on a fresh build of lib/dist: `buildBuddyGraph(120, 12)` returns in 110 ms with `polished === false` (budget refuses it), while `buildBuddyGraph(120, 12, { polish: true })` runs for 32788 ms and returns `polished === true`. This is reachable today from a file, not just from the lib API: `app/src/io/importGraph.ts:54` passes `s.polish === true` through untouched, `sanitizeSettings` clamps `buddies` to BUDDY_MAX = 12, and the app's mirror guard at `app/src/state/useBuddyGraph.ts:121` is `names.length > POLISH_MAX_N` with POLISH_MAX_N = 120 — which is FALSE at exactly 120. So a hostile BuddyGraph JSON with 120 people, `settings.buddies: 12`, `settings.polish: true` costs 33 s of worker time per Generate and per re-roll. The app's mirror is n-only because it was written against the OLD `n <= 120` gate; the core's gate became k-aware and the mirror did not, and the core's explicit-true escape hatch means the mirror was the only thing left guarding it.

gating.invariant: For every (n, k, options) that buildBuddyGraph or buildConstrainedBuddyGraph returns from, if the result reports `polished === true` then `polishWork(n, k, iters_actually_run) <= MAX_POLISH_WORK`. No value of `options.polish` may make this false.

gating.failure: `JSON.parse('{"polishIters":1e15}').polishIters` is 1e15, for which `Number.isInteger` is true and `< 0` is false, so `checkedIterations` returns it unchanged and it lands in `polish(g, { maxIters: 1e15 })`. Reproduced: `buildBuddyGraph(30, 4)` with the default 20000 iterations completes in 1220 ms; `buildBuddyGraph(30, 4, { polishIters: 1e15 })` did not return within a 25 s timeout (exit 124) — extrapolating the measured rate that is ~2 years. The constrained path is identical via `DEFAULT_CONSTRAINED_POLISH_ITERS`. Note also that `resolveWantPolish` deliberately gates on the DEFAULT iteration budget, so a hostile `polishIters` cannot even turn the polish gate off — auto-polish stays on at n=30,k=4 and then runs the attacker's count. The ratchet from the round that added this guard, `lib/test/optimizer.props.test.ts:247` (`for (const bad of [Infinity, NaN, -1, 1.5, -Infinity])`), is a case table, and 1e15 passes it by construction — exactly the failure mode the protocol names.

gating.invariant: For every (n, k, options), the number of polish iterations actually executed satisfies `polishWork(n, k, iters) <= MAX_POLISH_WORK` — for ALL values of `options.polishIters` and `options.polish`, not an enumerated set of malformed ones.

confirmed.theme: a size gate that runs after the work it is meant to bound — Constraints.fromTags builds O(n^2) pair keys inside the constructor, before validate can refuse anything
confirmed.summary: `Constraints.fromTags` takes `n` entirely on faith — unlike `degreeOf` in the same file, the `Graph` constructor and `validate`, all of which guard it — and then runs an unguarded `for (i < n) { for (j < n) }` materializing one Set key per same-tag pair, so the cost is paid before any cap can be consulted.
confirmed.failure: `fromTags(1e15, [])` enters `for (let i = 0; i < 1e15; i++)` with no guard whatsoever and never returns; `fromTags(3000, Array(3000).fill('A'))` spends ~3.4 s building 4.5M keys and at tens of millions of pairs the Set construction throws before `validate`'s MAX_CONSTRAINED_N refusal is ever reached. Also `NaN` as a tag value never equals itself, so `prohibit_same` silently produces no constraints for that group. Filed as a deferral, not gating: `grep` finds no caller of `fromTags` outside `lib/test` — the tag UI is P2 and explicitly deferred in app/CLAUDE.md — so nothing untrusted reaches it in the current tree, and this is already recorded in lib/CLAUDE.md's known-limitations list. Repeating it here only so the log is complete for this round.

confirmed.invariant: `Constraints.fromTags(n, tags, policy)` returns or throws in time O(n + emitted pairs) with emitted pairs <= a stated cap, for all n and all tags — it never performs work proportional to an unvalidated n.

observations.note: A critic left a scratch harness in the working tree: an untracked `lib/test/zz_frag.test.ts` that vitest then picked up. It ran for 90 s and timed out, so on the next `npm test` it read as two FAILING tests. Critics have Bash access by design (that is what lets them measure rather than speculate), and nothing told this one to clean up. Had it been committed it would have broken CI; had it been trusted it would have looked like a regression in the round-1 fix. Deleted, and the run is preserved in the session scratchpad.
observations.silverLining: Its output is the strongest evidence available for the round-1 fix: 432,954 fragmenting double-edge swaps examined over randomly structured disconnected graphs, zero of which lowered the objective. Recorded in optimizer.props.test.ts's header.

observations.note: Both blocking findings this round are against the round-1 fix, not against pre-existing code: MAX_POLISH_WORK was consulted only on the auto path, so an explicit `polish: true` re-opened the exact 33 s case it was introduced to close; and the new iteration guard checked type but not magnitude, so 1e15 passed where Infinity was caught. This is E1's self-reference tail, observed live and attributable by construction — the code they criticise was written one round earlier in this same loop.
